title: Path-integrated electrostatic energization in laser-driven collisionless cylindrical convergence
abstract:
Collisionless converging ion flows can sustain particle energization over an extended path, but the field channel responsible for the energy gain is not always identifiable. In laser-driven bladed microtube implosion, energetic carbon ions were previously observed alongside a self-generated gigagauss-class axial magnetic field [D. Pan and M. Murakami, ], leaving the origin of their energization unresolved. Using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, field-particle power decomposition and trajectory-resolved work accounting show that radial electrostatic work accumulated along the converging path supplies more than

title: Practical considerations in measuring out-of-field neutron dose for pulsed and gantry-mounted proton therapy machines
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Objective. 
                    Synchrocyclotrons deliver radiation in distinct macro pulses with high instantaneous dose rate that distinguish them from isochronous cyclotrons and synchrotrons. The relatively high instantaneous dose rates associated with synchrocyclotrons require special consideration in measurement of the neutron dose. The objective of this work is to measure the out-of-field neutron ambient dose equivalent (H*(10)) as a conservative operational surrogate to assess the fetal dose due to secondary neutrons for a gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron proton therapy system when an intensity modulated proton therapy (IMPT) brain treatment is delivered with the dynamic aperture (DA), static aperture (SA), and no aperture (NA).
                     Approach. 
                    A pencil beam scanning (PBS) gantry-mounted synchrocyclotron was used for beam delivery. IMPT plans employing the DA, SA, and NA, each with 3 fields (vertex, lateral, and posterior–anterior (PA)) were optimized using the treatment planning system to treat a left-sided spherical brain target with 6 cm diameter to a total dose of 66 Gy (weighted by radiobiological effectiveness [RBE] 1.1) in 33 fractions. The plans were delivered to an anthropomorphic phantom and the neutron H*(10) was measured using two commercial rem-meters, a WENDI-II and a LUPIN-BF3-NP counter at 43, 53, 61, and 71 cm distance from the isocenter intended to mimic distances to a fetus at various gestational periods. To investigate the influence of the couch angle for the PA field, the neutron dose from the PA field was measured at several couch angles including 0°, 180°, and 270°.
                     Main results. 
                    WENDI-II suffers from dead-time associated issues and underestimated the dose by a factor of ∼1.7–2.7 compared to LUPIN-BF3-NP. H*(10) showed dependence on the measurement location and the use of field shaping system. The total H*(10) for 66 Gy-equivalent proton dose was estimated to be 10.7 mSv (9.7 mSv) and 4.9 mSv (4.5 mSv) at 43 and 71 cm distance from the isocenter, respectively, when the SA (DA) was used. Without an aperture the corresponding values were 11.8 mSv and 5.3 mSv. The 270°-couch-angle resulted in the highest neutron dose from the PA field by ∼15% relative to the 0°-couch-angle, resulting in an increase in the neutron dose by ∼5% for the whole treatment.
                     Significance. 
                    WENDI-II is not a reliable device for in-room neutron dose measurement for synchrocyclotrons with high instantaneous dose rates. Employing appropriate use of the aperture system as well as avoiding the 270° couch angle for the PA field can minimize the neutron dose in the gantry-mounted system studied in this work.

title: A single radiation hard pixel detector for proton dosimetry, imaging, energy resolution and beam monitoring
abstract: Proton therapy enables highly conformal tumour irradiation by exploiting the Bragg peak. Clinical precision relies on detector systems that provide linearity, spatial resolution, radiation hardness, and, for ultra-high-dose-rate (FLASH) therapy, high dynamic range with sufficient temporal response. No compact all-in-one solution currently fulfils all these requirements. Here, we present pixelated gallium nitride (GaN) arrays as a multifunctional platform. These detectors exhibit high linearity (proton currents from 70 to 1700 pA cm-2) and signal uniformity below 2% across 128 pixels. To probe GaN radiation hardness, we applied cumulative doses up to 6.7 MGy at energies from 25 MeV down to the Bragg-peak regime. Locally deposited dose dictates long-term signal loss, yet devices preserve linearity and spatial response. We demonstrate 0.25 mm effective spatial resolution, validated against radiochromic film. Proton radiography resolves fine tissue structures, with the dose extrapolated to 7 mGy per 1 ms frame in a prospective single-shot configuration. Energy-dependent responses match GATE/Geant4 simulations, and wedge measurements enable Bragg-peak tracking with an energy resolution below 10 keV in an optimised geometry. Real-time ms-scale beam monitoring enables live dose verification.These results establish GaN pixel detectors as a scalable and radiation-hard platform, enabling dosimetry, beam monitoring and energy verification in one device.

title: Learning to reconstruct Germano Differential Filtered Fields with Convolutional Neural Networks for Large Eddy Simulation of Plasma Turbulence
abstract: We present a novel method which combines the invertibility of the differential filter of Germano, with convolutional networks to accelerate plasma turbulence simulations. Rather than learning the mapping from coarse-grid LES fields to fine-grid DNS, the proposed method learns the mapping from coarse LES fields to the differential-filtered DNS fields. We then use the inverse of Germano's filter to reconstruct the fine-scale details and hence calculate exactly the nonlinear terms in the governing equations and subgrid-scale terms in the LES equations. The method is tested on the 2D Hasegawa-Wakatani (HW) and modified Hasegawa-Wakatani (mHW) plasma turbulence models at $256^2$ and $512^2$ DNS resolutions using 2, 4 and 8 times smaller LES grids in each direction. We compare the model with DNS results on energy, enstrophy, spectra, probability distributions, poloidal and radial fluxes and computational cost. Validation extends to 1000 simulation time units for HW and 100 for mHW, whose faster dynamics lead toward laminarization. For the $256^2$ cases, the finer LES meshes preserve several integral and spectral features, whereas the coarsest mesh yields unphysical behavior. In contrast, for the $512^2$ cases, even the coarsest LES mesh preserves the turbulent character of the flow and maintains acceptable statistics for both the HW and mHW models. Moreover, we show how our methodology is superior to traditional algebraic numerical LES models, which traditionally fail to capture important design features. Finally, benchmarks show an MPI task-time reductions of 4.82--49.45, with a maximum wall-clock speedup of $1.55\times$ when compared to full CPU socket.

title: A modern particle-in-cell code for beam-beam simulations of future colliders
abstract: A key challenge in the design of next-generation colliders is predicting the effects of beam-beam interactions and using these predictions to optimize machine performance. Beam-beam interactions are characterized by strong focusing forces, radiative effects, and the generation of background particles. While analytical formulas provide insight into the dynamics of beam-beam interactions, these nonlinear, coupled effects are most accurately described with numerical methods. In this paper, we introduce the open-source particle-in-cell code WarpX as a modern tool for modeling the interaction point in future lepton colliders. WarpX provides high-performance execution on distributed GPU architectures within an open-source and actively maintained code base. We present convergence scans and benchmarks against the established beam-beam codes GUINEA-PIG (v1.2.2) and CAIN (v2.42) for luminosity spectra, photon emission, and secondary-particle production under a wide range of beam parameters corresponding to different collider concepts. Our results show that WarpX (v26.09) reproduces the benchmark beam-beam observables while enabling GPU-portable, extensible simulations. These results establish WarpX as a scalable platform for high-fidelity beam-beam modeling in future collider studies.

title: Programmable Hard-X-Ray Spectral Comb Generation via Laser-Compton Scattering
abstract: Independent control of line spacing and offset underpins programmable frequency-comb spectroscopy, yet it has not been established for hard-X-ray sources based on inverse Compton scattering after electron transport and angular collection. Self-consistent multi-particle tracking and Li'enard-Wiechert radiation calculations model a transported 10 pC beam and its angle-integrated spectrum near 11 keV. Laser pulse separation programs the comb spacing, while pulse-to-pulse phase translates the entire line grid at fixed spacing. The spacing model agrees within 0.52%, while transport and optics change the phase-transfer slope by less than 0.2%. At fixed electron spot size, the largest resolvable separation scales as the inverse square of normalized emittance; subnanometer bunches also produce a mode-locked train with 13.9 as spacing. This two-coordinate programmability enables phase-stepped multicolor measurements and offers routes to hard-X-ray Ramsey interferometry, coherent control of core and nuclear excitations, and attosecond nonlinear spectroscopy.
